Command: Do not eat or drink on the Day of Atonement
Summary: On the Day of Atonement, no food or drink may be taken; the fast is the form of afflicting the soul.
Commandment: On the Day of Atonement, eat no food and drink nothing.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The fast made the day's humbling bodily and total, matching the solemnity of atonement. Debated: some see the commanded observance fulfilled as shadow (Colossians 2:16-17); others keep feasts voluntarily as memorial, not as binding command. The site does not settle whether observance continues.
Purpose: To rehearse God's saving acts at appointed seasons (Leviticus 23); Paul calls Christ our Passover (1 Corinthians 5:7).
Function: On the Day of Atonement, no food or drink might be taken — the fast was the form of afflicting the soul, a ceremonial law of bodily humbling. Its goal was to make the day's repentance total, the body's hunger matching the heart's humbling while atonement was made. The evil was approaching the holiest day unmoved, fed and comfortable while the high priest bore the nation's sins inside. It restrained that by the fast: the empty stomach said what the mouth might not have said.
